claims.text: Adding a small amount of tungsten to high-entropy nanoalloys improves their structural stability at high temperature.
Adding a small amount of tungsten to high-entropy nanoalloys improves their chemical stability at high temperature.
An effective tungsten addition lies in the range of approximately 1–5 at.%.
The proposed benefit applies to high-temperature use above 800°C.
Tungsten addition can produce a stable, dispersed population of tungsten-rich nanoparticles.
Alternatively, tungsten addition can produce a stable tungsten-containing solid solution.
Tungsten has a high melting point and high thermal stability.
A stable tungsten-bearing phase hinders grain growth.
Tungsten addition reduces diffusion rates in the nanoalloy.
Tungsten addition decreases the formation of detrimental phases.
Tungsten addition improves oxidation resistance relative to an otherwise identically processed tungsten-free nanoalloy.
Tungsten addition improves corrosion resistance relative to an otherwise identically processed tungsten-free nanoalloy.
Tungsten addition improves resistance to microstructural degradation relative to an otherwise identically processed tungsten-free nanoalloy.
The improved stability increases high-temperature performance and service life.
The stability improvement remains significant up to approximately 1000°C.
Above approximately 1000°C, other degradation mechanisms may dominate.
The optimal tungsten concentration and operative mechanisms depend on the particular alloy composition and processing conditions.
The effects of tungsten addition on strength and ductility are not well understood.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that tungsten's effects on mechanical properties are not understood, but the falsification rule appears to require improved mechanical properties and may reject the hypothesis if such improvement is absent. Mechanical-property improvement is not clearly part of the central stability prediction.
